cohort.label: 2011–2013 City Council
cohort.transition_reason: December 5, 2011 municipal election swearing-in: Mayor Bill Bell and At-Large incumbents Eugene Brown and Diane Catotti re-elected; Steve Schewel sworn in At-Large replacing retiring Farad Ali. Ward 3 Council Member Mike Woodard resigned effective December 31, 2012 upon taking office in the North Carolina Senate, leaving a brief 6-member transition until Don Moffitt was seated on January 7, 2013. Don Moffitt appointed and seated on January 7, 2013 to complete the unexpired Ward 3 term of Mike Woodard.

conflicts.issue: 751 South Conditional 10-Year Annexation and Water/Sewer Extension Agreement (Item 24)
conflicts.summary: Council split 3-4 on whether to approve water and sewer extension and a conditional 10-year annexation for the 253-acre 751 South / Colvard Farms project under threat of NC General Assembly intervention.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the conditional agreement to lock in NC 751 road widening and secure a 10-year annexation charter amendment.
side_a_arguments: Mayor Bill Bell warned that state legislative leaders had stated in no uncertain terms that the General Assembly would force Durham to extend water and sewer if the city did not reach an agreement.
Without this agreement, Durham could be forced to provide utilities without developer-funded widening of NC 751 and without the 10-year annexation charter change to protect future city budgets.
Cora Cole-McFadden noted she distrusted the players but respected the Mayor's effort to salvage concessions, and Howard Clement III joined in voting yes.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the utility extension and conditional annexation on planning, environmental, legal, and anti-coercion grounds.
side_b_arguments: Diane Catotti noted the request grew from 167 to 253 acres (adding Colvard Farms) without an updated cost-benefit analysis, criticized the developers' absence, and cited past protest-petition and watershed-boundary maneuvers.
Don Moffitt argued the project undermined the comprehensive plan and drove sprawl toward Chatham County instead of transit-oriented growth near Page Road and I-40.
Eugene Brown and Steve Schewel condemned General Assembly 'extortion' and refusal to negotiate with a 'gun to our heads,' warning of Jordan Lake water-quality risks.
conflicts.resolution: Motion failed 3-4.

conflicts.issue: Item 21: Meadows at Southpoint Rezoning, Density, and Barbee Road / NC 54 Traffic
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 over approving the Meadows at Southpoint rezoning, falling one vote short of the six-vote supermajority required by a valid protest petition.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with newly modified roadway timing and $150,000 City of Durham transportation contribution commitments.
side_a_arguments: The applicant met repeatedly with neighbors over nearly a year, reduced density, dropped Tract 3, and made major concessions.
The I-40 corridor location is appropriate for density, and all proffered road improvements are tied prior to the first certificate of occupancy.
Blocking development leaves Barbee Road improvements unfunded because private land and developer contributions are part of fixing the corridor.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the rezoning in deference to impacted neighborhood residents and unresolved traffic and infrastructure concerns.
side_b_arguments: Nearby residents strongly opposed the proposed project and questioned whether future development could offer equal or different protections.
Traffic congestion and uncertainty around Barbee Road / NC 54 improvements and apartment impacts remained unresolved for the surrounding neighborhood.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to approve failed 5-2 at 03:10:21 (failing to reach the 6-vote supermajority required by the valid protest petition).

conflicts.issue: Funding Solid Waste Fleet Replacement via Monthly User Fee vs. Property Tax (Item 5d)
conflicts.summary: Council split 4-2 on establishing a monthly solid waste capital recovery fee to pay for sanitation truck fleet replacement, with two members arguing the flat fee is regressive compared to a property tax increase.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the monthly solid waste fee as proposed in the FY 2013-2014 budget to create a dedicated revenue stream for truck fleet replacement.
side_a_arguments: Provides dedicated funding for urgent solid waste truck fleet replacement.
Adopted as part of the balanced FY 2013-2014 budget package.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the flat monthly solid waste user fee and fund needed solid waste vehicles through the property tax instead.
side_b_arguments: A flat monthly fee on households is regressive compared to property taxation.
Both dissenting members supported purchasing the additional solid waste trucks but objected to the fee structure.
conflicts.resolution: Item 5(d) passed 4-2 as part of the Consent Agenda adoption of the FY 2013-2014 Budget, with Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel recorded as voting No.

conflicts.issue: Item 26 Deferral vs. Substantive Action on Rezoning and Utility/Annexation Planning Policy
conflicts.summary: Council deadlocked 3-3 on deferring Item 26 without opening the public hearing, pitting members seeking additional time for staff-applicant negotiations against members pressing established planning and utility-extension standards.
conflicts.side_a_position: Defer Item 26 rather than forcing an immediate deadlock or opening the public hearing only to re-advertise.
side_a_arguments: With Council at loggerheads, additional time between meetings could allow the applicant and staff to reach a workable resolution.
Opening a public hearing without continuing to a compliant advertised date would require re-advertising.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose deferral and maintain consistent planning scrutiny over rezoning, annexation, and utility extension agreements.
side_b_arguments: Flagging utility extension agreements, annexation, and rezoning consistency reflects long-standing responsible Joint City-County Planning Committee policy predating the 751 assemblage.
Concerns remained over peripheral growth along Fayetteville Road south of I-40 from Parkwood to the Orange County line.
conflicts.resolution: Motion to defer failed 3-3; with no consensus to open the public hearing or advance an alternative motion, Council acknowledged the deadlock and moved to the next item.

conflicts.summary: Motion to authorize the City Manager to execute the utility extension agreement between Southern Durham Development and the City for the 751 Assemblage; Diane Catotti moved the item with the stated intention of voting no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 0-6)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (0-6)

conflicts.issue: Urban Bow Hunting of Deer Ordinance Amendment (Consent Item 9)
conflicts.summary: Council Member Diane Catotti registered formal personal disapproval of the deer bow-hunting ordinance amendment on the consent agenda while voting yes solely because state law required unanimity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the ordinance amendment permitting bow hunting of deer under state statutory framework.
side_a_arguments: Requires unanimous council support under state law to proceed.
conflicts.side_b_position: Personally oppose bow hunting of deer within city limits while declining to unilaterally veto the measure.
side_b_arguments: Registered personal dissatisfaction with the item on the record while voting yes so as not to block the unanimous requirement.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-0 as part of the consent agenda.

conflicts.issue: Carolina Crossing II Seven-Story Medical Office Rezoning at NC 54 & Farrington Road (Z12-00004)
conflicts.summary: Following an 8-4 Planning Commission denial recommendation and Falconbridge neighborhood opposition to building height and severe congestion at NC 54/Farrington Road, Council debated whether $1 million in interim road improvements and a new pedestrian-crossing proffer justified approving two seven-story medical office buildings.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with $1 million in interim roadway improvements and proffered pedestrian crosswalks/signals.
side_a_arguments: City and NCDOT traffic staff verified the developer's interim turn lanes and median improvements would maintain Level of Service D and improve intersection efficiency for a decade or more before NCDOT's $40M flyover is funded.
The applicant's last-minute proffer of crosswalks and pedestrian signals addressed TTA transit rider safety across NC 54.
The site lies in a compact neighborhood tier near a future transit station node.
conflicts.side_b_position: Opposed by Planning Commission (8-4) and Falconbridge residents (Van Noah, Rosemary Kitchen, Julia McMillan) due to traffic congestion, cut-through volume, and seven-story scale.
side_b_arguments: NC 54 and Farrington Road is already one of the region's most congested intersections, and two medical office towers generate roughly 40 times the weekday traffic of the existing church.
Two seven-story buildings are aesthetically out of scale with surrounding one- to three-story structures and will worsen neighborhood cut-through traffic on Hunting Ridge Road.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-0 after the applicant proffered pedestrian crosswalk and signal improvements at NC 54 and Farrington Road.

conflicts.issue: Living Wage Requirements and City-County Cost Sharing in Concord Hospitality Incentive Agreement (Item 12)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-1 over whether to approve a $1.33 million historic-preservation incentive for Concord Hospitality's Residence Inn at McPherson Hospital when roughly half of the hotel's permanent positions would pay below Durham's $11.91 living wage.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reluctantly approve the incentive to save the historic McPherson Hospital building, add 143 downtown hotel rooms, and gain net tax revenue.
side_a_arguments: The 1926 McPherson Hospital has no historic protection and would likely deteriorate or be demolished without the incentive.
City policy only mandates living wages for job-creation incentives and city-service contracts, not capital/historic preservation grants, and prior hotel incentives did not impose living wages.

Concord committed to good-faith local hiring via Durham JobLink, competitive benefits, and wage growth above $11.91 over time, though council members urged future policy reform on living wages and county cost-sharing.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose or defer the incentive unless all jobs meet Durham's living-wage standard.
side_b_arguments: Public tax dollars should not subsidize private projects that exclude service workers from a living wage.
Clement urged a two-cycle deferral to ask Concord Hospitality to incorporate living-wage compliance into the agreement.
conflicts.resolution: Incentive agreement approved 5-1 with Howard Clement III voting no.

conflicts.issue: Removal of Local Historic Landmark Designation for Liberty Warehouses No. 1 and No. 2 (Case LD1200003)
conflicts.summary: A sharp policy debate arose over whether City Council should revoke the local historic landmark designation of Liberty Warehouses No. 1 and No. 2 to facilitate a $50 million private redevelopment based on a negotiated developer-Preservation Durham compromise, overriding the Historic Preservation Commission's unanimous denial recommendation.
conflicts.side_a_position: De-list Liberty Warehouse as a local historic landmark to enable East West Partners' $50 million mixed-use redevelopment and Preservation Durham memorialization compromise, while reforming the HPC process separately.
side_a_arguments: Adaptive reuse of the deteriorated 200,000 sq ft warehouse is economically infeasible after years of failed attempts and a 2011 roof collapse.
Preservation Durham negotiated a compromise retaining the southern brick wall, northeastern facade, signs, and old wood, and documenting tobacco auction history.
Redevelopment brings $50M investment, workforce housing, Central Park connectivity, and ~$850,000/year in city real estate and sales taxes.
Landmark designation only delays demolition by one year anyway, and waiting further will not save the building.
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the de-listing application under UDO Section 3.17 criteria, keep review within public Historic Preservation Commission channels, and maintain enforcement against demolition by neglect.
side_b_arguments: Liberty Warehouse remains Durham's last surviving downtown tobacco auction house and still meets cultural and architectural landmark criteria (unanimous HPC, Planning staff, and SHPO finding).
De-listing based on a developer's redevelopment proposal rather than objective historic merit undermines the entire local landmark program.
Removing landmark status eliminates binding preservation commitments and relies on private negotiations held outside public HPC review.

Critics questioned why $500/day demolition-by-neglect fines against Greenfire were stayed and argued owners should face interest/penalties when repaying tax benefits (a point Moffitt echoed for future ordinance reform).
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 6-0 to de-list Liberty Warehouses No. 1 and No. 2; Don Moffitt requested future ordinance changes to assess interest/penalties on repaid tax credits, and Steve Schewel noted ongoing Planning staff focus groups to rebuild confidence in the HPC process.

conflicts.issue: Item 18: Southpoint Trails Rezoning (4-3 Split Vote)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 on approving the Southpoint Trails zoning map change, reflecting ongoing division over residential density increases south of I-40.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Southpoint Trails rezoning.
side_a_arguments: A four-member majority supported advancing the rezoning (specific floor arguments truncated in digest).
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the Southpoint Trails rezoning.
side_b_arguments: Don Moffitt and Steve Schewel (along with a third unnamed member) voted against the rezoning, consistent with concerns voiced at the February 7 work session regarding density increases south of I-40 without a compelling exception.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 4-3 (with Don Moffitt, Steve Schewel, and one unnamed member voting No; valid protest petition did not apply because the Clerk ruled the petition invalid).

conflicts.issue: Statewide Bail Bond / Pretrial Release Legislative Proposal for Repeat Firearm Offenses
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-1 on a proposed statewide general statute amendment restricting magistrate pretrial release for individuals on pretrial release for a weapons offense who are charged with a second weapons offense, with Steve Schewel dissenting on effectiveness and constitutional grounds.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support including the statewide pretrial release amendment in the City's legislative agenda.
side_a_arguments: Judges remain directly involved in setting bond when appropriate under the proposed statewide statutory amendment.
Monitoring individuals on pretrial release for weapons offenses provides critical data on court appearance rates, offense severity, and re-offending currently unavailable to local officials.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the bail bond / pretrial release legislative proposal.
side_b_arguments: Even in revised form, the proposal will not have an impact because judges already take repeat weapons offenses seriously and no data shows they fail to exercise appropriate discretion.
Constitutional principles prohibit punitive bail before guilt or innocence is established, limiting pretrial detention to ensuring court appearance and community safety.
Bail amounts would still ultimately be set despite the procedural delay.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-1 on the Consent Agenda (Steve Schewel recorded as voting No; Howard Clement III absent), with the proposal advancing to the Crime Cabinet.

conflicts.issue: Homeless Services Advisory Committee Slot Appointments
conflicts.summary: Mike Woodard sought to bundle two Homeless Services Advisory Committee appointments into one motion, drawing objection from a colleague supporting Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden's position and leading Mayor Bill Bell to split the votes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the corporate-sector/Duke-slot appointment alongside reappointing Chris Toole to the nonprofit slot and re-advertising the remaining vacancy.
side_a_arguments: The committee slot has been open for a while and Duke holds a designated seat on the Homeless Services Advisory Committee.
Splitting the motion allows members to vote separately on each candidate.
conflicts.side_b_position: Support Chris Toole's reappointment to the nonprofit slot while opposing the bundled corporate-sector/Duke-slot appointment.
side_b_arguments: Bundling both appointments forces members who support Chris Toole to vote against their preference on the other slot.
Aligning with Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden's opposition to the Duke-slot nominee.
conflicts.resolution: Motion was split: Chris Toole's reappointment passed unanimously by voice vote, and the corporate-sector appointment passed by voice vote with at least one dissenting 'No' vote (individual names not recorded in voice vote).

conflicts.issue: Homeless Services Advisory Committee Slot Assignments (Cara Johansson & Kimmeline Monroe)
conflicts.summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden sought to place Duke employee Kimmeline Monroe into Duke's designated seat so Cara Johansson could retain a second-term seat without re-advertising, but a 4-member majority defeated the motion 3-4.
conflicts.side_a_position: Appoint Kimmeline Monroe to the Duke slot (with Dr. Nguyen's agreement) and reappoint Cara Johansson to the remaining slot for a second term without re-advertising.
side_a_arguments: Dr. Nguyen agreed to appoint Kimmeline Monroe, a Duke employee, to the Duke slot.
Council normally allows appointees to serve at least two terms and avoids unnecessary re-advertising.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the proposed slot reassignment and reappointment motion (exact arguments of the four Nay voters are not detailed in the digest).
side_b_arguments: Four councilmembers voted Nay on the electronic ballot, with the seconder noting the prevailing direction of the Council before seconding.
conflicts.resolution: Motion failed 3-4; one additional Aye voter and the four Nay voters were not named in the transcript.

conflicts.issue: Economic Development Incentive Agreement (Item 25)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-1 on approving an economic development incentive agreement (scheduled on the April 2 agenda as Item 25 with Self-Help Venture Fund) after the City Attorney defended its statutory validity.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the economic development incentive agreement.
side_a_arguments: City Attorney advised the agreement qualified as an authorized municipal economic development deal capable of withstanding legal challenge.
Supporting member noted personal connection to Durham Public Schools through his wife's 16 years teaching, but stated voting for the agreement was the right decision.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the economic development incentive agreement.
side_b_arguments: Dissenting vote cast against approving the agreement (specific floor remarks occurred prior to the truncated middle section).
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-1, with Steve Schewel voting No.

conflicts.issue: Excused Absence Request for Council Member Howard Clement III
conflicts.summary: Council divided 5-1 on granting an excused absence to Council Member Howard Clement III at the start of the December 19 meeting.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve excused absence for Howard Clement III
side_a_arguments: Excused absence requested prior to roll call and supported by five members
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose excusing the absence
side_b_arguments: Voted no without extended floor remarks in the transcript digest
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-1

conflicts.issue: Farrington Road Residential Suburban-10 Rezoning and School/Environmental Impacts
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-1 to approve straight R-10 rezoning on Farrington Road after public opponents pushed for a PDR zoning alternative to protect New Hope Creek wetlands and Council Member Mike Woodard raised Durham Public Schools capacity mitigation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the straight R-10 rezoning as recommended by Planning staff and the Planning Commission
side_a_arguments: Consistent with the Durham Comprehensive Plan and unanimously recommended (12-0) by the Planning Commission
Applicant Bill Ripley stated his proposed six-lot layout would maintain lot sizes between 18,900 and 25,000 square feet under lot averaging
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose straight R-10 rezoning without binding protections or PDR clustering
side_b_arguments: Straight R-10 zoning could yield up to eight lots and add one Durham Public Schools student without enforceable school-donation or layout conditions
Public opponents warned straight R-10 increases impervious surface and threatens steep slopes and New Hope Creek wetlands compared to neighboring PDR developments
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-1

conflicts.issue: Roadside Solicitation Ordinance Revisions and Travel-Lane Safety
conflicts.summary: Council debated Homeless Services Advisory Committee (HSAC) proposals to relax portions of Durham's roadside solicitation ordinance, splitting between easing restrictions on solicitors and maintaining strict prohibitions against entering travel lanes or approaching driver-side windows.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support relaxing portions of the roadside solicitation ordinance in line with HSAC recommendations
side_a_arguments: Avoids overly punitive restrictions on panhandlers and addresses concerns raised in court proceedings
Incorporates months of collaborative work and recommendations from HSAC members directly engaged with homelessness issues
conflicts.side_b_position: Maintain strict street-safety rules barring solicitation in travel lanes and on driver-side vehicle approaches while tackling root causes
side_b_arguments: Placing panhandlers, student carwash bucket brigades, or any pedestrians in active travel lanes alongside 3,000-pound vehicles is unsafe
Approaching vehicles from the driver's side creates traffic hazards, and residential corridors like Club Boulevard and Duke Street need protection
HSAC's recommendations are not fully developed legally and require City Attorney drafting rather than weakening existing safety provisions
conflicts.resolution: No ordinance vote was taken; Council directed the City Attorney's office to work with staff and HSAC contributors to review legal options and draft specific language.

conflicts.issue: Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Grade Separations, Street Closures, and State Funding Strategy (Item 9)
conflicts.summary: Public urban-design advocates, county officials, and residents clashed with the draft Traffic Separation Study's crossing closure and concrete grade-separation proposals, while council members differed on the realism of state rail funding versus entering the NCDOT scoring pipeline.
conflicts.side_a_position: Reject proposed crossing closures and concrete retaining-wall grade separations, and question the viability of state rail funding.
side_a_arguments: Durham Area Designers (Dan Jewell, Randy Hester, Eric Hite, Robin Heeks) argued concrete channels and 12-foot retaining walls would recreate a physical barrier through downtown and destroy pedestrian connectivity.
Deputy County Manager Lee Worsley warned Dillard Street closure would harm county operations and EMS response times, while Gwen Silver and James Chavis warned of isolating East Durham.
Council Member Eugene Brown argued state transportation funding is shrinking due to fuel-efficient cars and predicted light rail and grade-separation funds would remain a low-priority footnote.
conflicts.side_b_position: Treat the draft study as an initial engineering 'straw man' and position downtown crossings for state freight-rail scoring without committing to street closures.
side_b_arguments: Future freight and commuter/light rail expansion requires planning now rather than leaving downtown crossings unprotected.

Entering the NCDOT statewide freight tier (40% of state transportation funding) is the only realistic funding stream for the shared rail corridor, while reserving final decisions on closures and urban design for crossing-by-crossing feasibility studies.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 5-0 to refer public comments back to staff without endorsing long-term closures, requesting short-term safety recommendations.

conflicts.issue: UDI CDC Sewer Assessment Waiver Dispute on East Cornwallis Road (Item 11)
conflicts.summary: UDI Community Development Corporation contested a sewer assessment on 4601 Industry Lane citing P.O. Box notice issues, a prior easement swap, and pre-existing sewer access, prompting Council to defer the parcel.
conflicts.side_a_position: Waive the sewer assessment against 4601 Industry Lane (argued by UDI CDC President Ed Stewart; engineering staff confirmed UDI already had rear sewer access).
side_a_arguments: UDI did not receive mailed hearing notices sent to a closed P.O. Box and had been told an earlier easement land swap carried no cost.
Engineering staff testified that 4601 Industry Lane already had access to an existing sewer outfall and gained no additional benefit.
conflicts.side_b_position: Confirm other assessments (11B) while continuing UDI's parcel (11C) four weeks to clarify maps, easement swap history, and relief eligibility.
side_b_arguments: Council lacked maps and sufficient documentation on the land swap and whether an unconnected parcel with pre-existing availability qualifies for relief until tap-on.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 5-0 (Mayor Bell recused) to confirm Item 11B and continue Item 11C for four weeks.

conflicts.issue: City-County Interlocal Funding for Sheriff's Warrant Control and Joint Planning Department
conflicts.summary: Council members discussed Durham County Commissioners' dissatisfaction over the end of city funding for the warrant backlog program and potential county cuts to the joint City-County Planning Department, weighing independent city planning funding against preserving interlocal cooperation.
conflicts.side_a_position: If Durham County reduces its share of joint Planning Department funding over the warrant program dispute, the City should step in to fund long-range planning independently rather than let planning capacity shrink.
side_a_arguments: The city fulfilled its multi-year commitment to eliminate the warrant backlog and is doing more planning within city jurisdiction.
Under the interlocal structure, a county funding cut triggers a comparable city cut unless addressed, threatening critical long-range planning such as affordable housing around future transit stops.
conflicts.side_b_position: Avoid escalating an interlocal battle with Durham County government and clarify administrative communication regarding agreements.
side_b_arguments: Durham faces sufficient policy challenges from Raleigh and Washington, D.C., and needs City-County unity for all residents.
County Commissioners reportedly felt unaware that the warrant agreement had ended, indicating a need for clearer communication between administrations and elected boards.
conflicts.resolution: Informational discussion only; Item 20 (FY14 Planning Department Work Program) had been referred back to City Administration for revision and return in August.

conflicts.issue: Item 24: Consolidated Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement — 751 South
conflicts.summary: Planning and Legal staff presented the 253-acre 751 South / Colvard Farms utility extension and conditional 10-year annexation (effective June 3, 2023), made contingent on the General Assembly passing a charter amendment extending Durham's deferral window from 3 to 10 years and requiring the developer to widen NC 751. Six speakers—Helen Fisher, Steve Bocckino, Susan Sewell, Donna Rudolph, Carolyn Aaronson, and Tom Miller—opposed the deal over Jordan Lake watershed runoff, traffic, lack of statutory authority before charter passage, and legislative extortion, while Victoria Peterson urged approval for jobs and tax revenue. Mayor Bill Bell, Howard Clement III, and Cora Cole-McFadden supported the agreement as the best way to secure NC 751 widening and charter protection before expected legislative coercion, whereas Diane Catotti, Don Moffitt, Eugene Brown, and Steve Schewel voted no, citing comprehensive plan violations, the addition of Colvard Farms without updated fiscal analysis, developer absence, and refusal to yield to General Assembly threats. Catotti moved the item with the stated intent to vote no, and it failed 3-4.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-4)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-4)

conflicts.issue: Scope of Council Action on the Draft Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS)
conflicts.summary: Council members questioned whether a future resolution on the Traffic Separation Study should endorse long-term rail grade-separation projects and street closures or only receive the report and endorse near-term priorities pending downtown planning.
conflicts.side_a_position: Limit formal endorsement to short- and mid-term improvements while treating long-term grade separations conceptually until coordinated with downtown planning and funding
side_a_arguments: Endorsing long-term street closures and pedestrian overpasses before the October 24 Downtown Vision Workshop and Urban Open Space Plan is premature
Grade separations heavily impact the urban environment and require separate public involvement and funding clarity amid shifting NCDOT formulas
conflicts.side_b_position: Endorse a prioritized project list so staff can pursue state and federal rail-corridor funding
side_b_arguments: Merely receiving the report without endorsing a priority list weakens Durham's competitive standing for NCDOT State Tier and federal funding
Endorsing the study's priority list still requires individual Council resolutions and public input before any street is actually closed
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to incorporate Council feedback after the October 21 public hearing and refine the proposed resolution language before returning in December.

conflicts.issue: Downtown Parking General Fund Subsidy, Residential Permits & Ninth Street Paid Parking
conflicts.summary: During review of the Downtown and Ninth Street parking studies, Council members expressed competing priorities over continuing the $2 million annual General Fund parking subsidy, how much to charge downtown residents for garage permits (including covered vs. surface spaces), and whether paid on-street parking on Ninth Street would harm local merchants.
conflicts.side_a_position: Question the $2 million parking subsidy relative to transit and affordable housing, and preserve Ninth Street lot access while holding the lease item briefly
side_a_arguments: Subsidizing $2 million a year for downtown parking represents an opportunity cost against competing priorities like transit fares and affordable housing
An off-street lot on Ninth Street is critical to East-side merchants, while on-street paid parking will not drive away customers despite 450-500 petition emails
Covered garage spaces warrant full-rate pricing compared to half-price surplus surface parking
conflicts.side_b_position: Support maintaining downtown parking affordability/incentives, examine 'first hour free' and employee permits, and investigate historical 1992 free-parking claims
side_b_arguments: Downtown residents raised concerns about $55-$65 monthly rates and 8 a.m.-6 p.m. off-peak restrictions
Clarifying whether any 1992 resolution promised free parking and evaluating a first-hour-free option or Ninth Street employee permits could soften merchant and resident impacts
conflicts.resolution: No final vote on parking rates was taken; Item 17 was referred back to administration and staff agreed to provide the 1992 resolution history and additional modeling.

conflicts.issue: FY 2013-14 Budget Revenue Strategy: Property Tax vs. Solid Waste Fee and Bus Fare Increases
conflicts.summary: During the budget E-Town Hall and public hearing, council members and residents debated whether to replace the proposed $18 annual solid waste fee and $0.50 bus day-pass hike with a modest property tax increase.
conflicts.side_a_position: Eliminate the solid waste fee and bus day-pass increase and fund them (plus employee pay/trails) with less than a one-cent property tax increase.
side_a_arguments: Council Member Steve Schewel and speakers from People's Alliance, Durham CAN, and People's Durham argued the $18 solid waste fee and $0.50 bus day-pass increase are regressive and disproportionately harm low-income renters and transit-dependent families.

Property taxes are progressive and federally deductible for itemizers, unlike municipal fees, and less than one penny on the tax rate could cover the bus pass, solid waste fee, Ellerbe Creek Trail, and employee pay.
conflicts.side_b_position: Keep property taxes flat and evaluate fee-for-service benchmarking against peer cities.
side_b_arguments: Mayor Bill Bell noted that Council directed the City Manager to propose a balanced budget without a property tax increase and pointed out that peer North Carolina cities fund services through user fees rather than relying solely on property taxes.
Council Member Don Moffitt noted fees charge service users directly while property taxes spread costs across the whole community.
conflicts.resolution: Public hearing closed 7-0; final budget and fee decisions deferred to the June 6 budget work session and subsequent adoption vote.

conflicts.issue: 2013 Long Session Legislative Agenda — Pretrial Release / Bail Restrictions for Firearm Offenders
conflicts.summary: Mayor Bill Bell and Council Member Steve Schewel differed over whether Durham should seek a state legislative amendment restricting pretrial release for repeat gun offenders.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support requesting a narrow statewide amendment to pretrial release laws targeting repeat firearm offenders.
side_a_arguments: Addresses a perceived revolving-door problem at the jail raised by residents and the Violent Crime Reduction Roundtable.
Narrowly targets individuals already on pretrial release or convicted within five years of an offense involving illegal firearm use, possession, or discharge.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose submitting the draft bail/pretrial release legislation to the General Assembly.
side_b_arguments: Local judges already make sound bail decisions and judicial discretion should be preserved.
Even a narrowly tailored Durham bill could be expanded by state legislators with a different agenda once introduced in the General Assembly.
conflicts.resolution: Discussed at work session without a vote; item moved off consent to the General Business Agenda for consideration at the regular meeting.

conflicts.issue: Item 26: Motion to Defer Without Opening Public Hearing
conflicts.summary: Following the failure of a substitute motion, the original motion to defer Item 26 tied 3-3 and failed.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-3)

conflicts.issue: Proposed Transit Fare Increases and Senior/Student Half-Fare Policy
conflicts.summary: Council members debated whether to consider bus fare increases and charging seniors and youth half-fare to help offset a projected $1.6M–$1.7M FY14 transit deficit.
conflicts.side_a_position: Support testing modest fare increases (such as a 10-cent base fare increase) and gathering public forum feedback to help close the transit budget gap.
side_a_arguments: A 10-cent fare increase would not fill the full $1.3M–$1.6M gap alone, but riders should contribute something rather than placing the entire burden on taxpayers.
A dime increase is unlikely to cause severe ridership losses, and public forums would provide data before May budget decisions.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose raising fares on existing riders and especially oppose charging seniors and students without specific local data.
side_b_arguments: Fare elasticity disproportionately pushes the poorest riders off transit first.
Changing free-fare policies for seniors and youth was not clearly flagged in earlier briefings and lacks specific local ridership impact data.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; City Manager clarified the discussion was to inform whether TTA should hold public comment forums ahead of May budget recommendations.

conflicts.issue: Operation Breakthrough CDBG Funding Exclusion in FY 2012-13 Annual Action Plan
conflicts.summary: Following Durham County's request to fund Operation Breakthrough's senior weatherization program ($75,000), councilmembers debated whether past scoring history justified reconsideration before uniting behind the Citizens Advisory Committee's 13-0 denial and competitive scoring audit rules.
conflicts.side_a_position: Uphold the original Annual Action Plan recommendation denying CDBG funding based on the 33/100 application score and unanimous CAC vote.
side_a_arguments: The 13-member Citizens Advisory Committee voted unanimously against funding Operation Breakthrough.
Awarding $75,000 to an application scoring 33/100 over higher-scoring rejected applicants would undermine HUD compliance and repeat deficiencies flagged in a prior city CDBG performance audit.
conflicts.side_b_position: Clarify how Operation Breakthrough applied and scored in prior years (e.g., non-construction vs. construction grant) before finalizing rejection.
side_b_arguments: Operation Breakthrough's director stated they applied as a non-construction grant and could not provide construction-grant documentation.
Reviewing past-year applications and scores could clarify the discrepancy without immediately committing $75,000.
conflicts.resolution: Council suspended the rules and voted unanimously by voice vote to approve the original staff/CAC Annual Action Plan without adding Operation Breakthrough.

conflicts.issue: Re-Advertising Durham Housing Authority Board Seat vs. Evaluating Remaining Applicant
conflicts.summary: Following the withdrawal of one applicant for the Durham Housing Authority Board, Council split 4-1 on whether to re-advertise the seat due to concerns about executive experience.
conflicts.side_a_position: Re-advertise the DHA Board seat to seek candidates with executive management experience
side_a_arguments: The Durham Housing Authority operates as a $30-$40 million-per-year enterprise
Re-advertising allows Council to recruit applicants with experience running an organization of that scale
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose rejecting the sole remaining candidate over perceived age or experience rather than simply enlarging the pool
side_b_arguments: Durham should encourage 'young blood' on boards rather than screening out newer applicants
Expanding the applicant pool is acceptable, but rejecting the candidate on experience grounds is objectionable
conflicts.resolution: Passed 4-1 by unattributed voice vote after suspending the rules (5-0) once Eugene Brown arrived.

conflicts.issue: Item 21: Zoning Map Change — Meadows at Southpoint
conflicts.summary: Initially tallied 6-1 before Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden's No vote was confirmed alongside Mayor Bill Bell's No vote, resulting in 5-2 failure because the valid protest petition required six affirmative votes.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 5-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (5-2)

conflicts.issue: Item 18: Zoning Map Change — Southpoint Trails
conflicts.summary: Passed 4-3; Don Moffitt and Steve Schewel were announced as voting No.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Selection of Durham Community Land Trustees (DCLT) to Negotiate Southside Project (Item 18)
conflicts.summary: Council voted 5-1 on a voice vote to authorize staff negotiations with Durham Community Land Trustees on the Southside project after an omitted middle discussion and expressions of concern about terms and conditions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Authorize staff to negotiate with DCLT and bring back a complete financing and deal package, potentially with time-limited conditions.
side_a_arguments: Authorizing negotiations does not bind the city to a final business deal until financing returns to Council.
Time conditions or renewal terms can be incorporated when staff returns with the formal agreement.
conflicts.side_b_position: One member opposed moving forward with the authorization at the work session.
side_b_arguments: Concerns were raised prior to the vote regarding moving ahead before the deal structure was settled.
conflicts.resolution: Passed 5-1 by voice vote among the six participating members (Howard Clement III excused absent); individual Aye/Nay voters were not named in the transcript digest.

conflicts.issue: Inclusion of Bars and Nightclubs in Outdoor Dining Permit Ordinance (Item 22)
conflicts.summary: Council and staff debated whether the proposed city code amendment for sidewalk outdoor dining permits should remain limited to restaurants or be expanded to include bars, nightclubs, and private clubs.
conflicts.side_a_position: Limit initial ordinance to restaurants to mitigate noise, late-night rowdy behavior, and enforcement concerns.
side_a_arguments: Police Chief Lopez and City Manager Bonfield expressed concern over late-night noise and public safety issues outside bars and nightclubs.
Staff noted state-maintained downtown streets are excluded and sidewalks require six-foot ADA clearance, limiting eligible locations.
conflicts.side_b_position: Include bars and nightclubs in the outdoor dining ordinance while strengthening permit revocation and enforcement tools.
side_b_arguments: Speakers cited Jane Jacobs and argued active downtown sidewalks improve safety and support well-run local businesses and jobs.
Supporters noted no pattern of problems had been shown at downtown bars and suggested adding clearer parameters for revoking permits under Section 54-141.
conflicts.resolution: Staff and the City Attorney were asked to review enforcement and revocation language to include bars and nightclubs, and action was held over to a subsequent cycle.

conflicts.issue: Hawthorne Durham LLC $1M Economic Development Incentive Outside Target Areas (Item 21)
conflicts.summary: Following a public hearing on a proposed $1 million economic development incentive for Hawthorne Durham LLC in the Urban Growth Area, an unidentified councilmember spoke against amending Durham's economic development policy outside community development target areas.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $1 million incentive over seven years to spur Urban Growth Area redevelopment and job creation.
side_a_arguments: Staff and public supporters cited an estimated 690 total jobs (307 permanent, 320 construction) and Durham JobLink workforce hiring commitments.
Staff noted no financial risk to the city if contractual performance benchmarks are not met.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the incentive and avoid amending economic development policy outside community development target areas.
side_b_arguments: An opposing councilmember stated they had consistently opposed the incentive in closed session and remained unwilling to amend economic development policy outside target areas.
conflicts.resolution: Item 21 was moved and seconded at 00:49:43, but the final vote outcome is omitted in the truncated middle portion of the transcript digest.

conflicts.issue: Contract SR-54 Utility Easement Mowing Bid Award ($200,000 Price Differential)
conflicts.summary: Water Management staff recommended bypassing lowest bidder TruGreen for the second-lowest bidder due to unverified easement-mowing references, while councilmembers questioned paying $200,000 more without senior staff personally verifying TruGreen's additional references.
conflicts.side_a_position: Award Contract SR-54 to the second-lowest bidder because TruGreen's submitted references have not been verified as comparable utility-easement maintenance.
side_a_arguments: The 200-mile contract crosses thousands of residential backyards requiring specialized bush-hogging and hand-cutting.
Initial reference checks showed no easement maintenance, and staff had not yet reached follow-up contacts by phone.
conflicts.side_b_position: Require senior staff (Mr. Greeley or department leadership) to personally verify TruGreen's references and provide definitive justification before spending $200,000 extra.
side_b_arguments: TruGreen representatives cited comparable right-of-way and utility easement mowing at Fort Hood, Gwinnett County, and Quantico Marine Base.
Council expects a definitive justification if the city is asked to pay $200,000 more for the second-lowest bidder.
conflicts.resolution: Staff agreed to personally follow up on the references and report back with a definitive recommendation before the Council votes at the regular meeting.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Bill Bell, the Durham City Council opened with reflections on recent fatal incidents—including a statement by Council Member Steve Schewel urging the State Bureau of Investigation, medical examiner, and district attorney to complete pending investigations into the deaths of Hsu Soreta, Carlos Riley, Jose O'Kompa, and Derek Walker—and a mayoral resolution declaring November 22, 2013 a day of solemn remembrance for President John F. Kennedy. Council suspended the rules to unanimously reappoint a member to the Triangle Transit Board of Trustees ahead of a November 30 term expiration, heard a public proposal from a transportation planner to revise the Durham-Orange Light Rail alignment to eliminate 18 at-grade crossings, and received the FY 2013-14 first-quarter financial report showing sales tax revenues $800,000 ahead of the prior year and $1 million in projected general fund salary savings alongside water/sewer weather shortfalls and a $2 million downtown parking subsidy. Council also appointed Megan Wisely to the Workforce Development Board and Alexia Klein-Stuber to the Open Space and Trails Commission (6 votes), and passed all procedural motions—including closed session and agenda-setting—unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: SBI Investigations Statement & JFK Day of Remembrance Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following presentation of a third-place Digital Cities survey award, Council Member Steve Schewel expressed condolences over the death of Hsu Soreta and urged the SBI, medical examiner, and district attorney to finish investigations into four pending cases (including Carlos Riley, Jose O'Kompa, and Derek Walker) so families and the community can get answers. Mayor Bill Bell also introduced a resolution proclaiming November 22, 2013 a day of solemn remembrance for President John F. Kennedy.

agenda_items.title: Closed Session Priority Request & Triangle Transit Board Reappointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously approved the City Attorney's priority request for a closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3). Council then voted unanimously to suspend the rules and reappoint the Triangle Transit Board of Trustees member whose term expired November 30 before Council's next regular meeting on December 2.

agenda_items.title: Durham-Orange Light Rail Grade-Crossing Alternative Proposal
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A Raleigh-based transportation planner addressed Council during Citizens Matters to propose an alignment revision for the Durham-Orange Light Rail project during Triangle Transit's NEPA review. The speaker argued the alternative would avoid roughly 18 new railroad grade crossings, addressing a major NCDOT safety concern for vehicles and pedestrians.

agenda_items.title: FY 2013-14 First Quarter Financial Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget staff reported first-quarter general fund performance, noting sales tax collections in October and November ran $800,000 ahead of the prior year and operating expenditures were projected $1 million under budget largely due to lapsed salaries across emergency communications, police, parks, and public works. Across enterprise funds, staff highlighted lower water/sewer irrigation revenues due to wet weather, transit fund property-tax timing, initial solid waste fee collections, a self-sufficient stormwater fund, a $2 million general fund subsidy for parking, and 59% general fund support for the ballpark fund.

agenda_items.title: Board Appointments & Setting the Regular Meeting Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Clerk announced the appointments of Megan Wisely to the Workforce Development Board and Alexia Klein-Stuber (with 6 votes) to the Open Space and Trails Commission. Council then unanimously set the regular meeting agenda (consent Items 1-2, 4-15, and 17-19; GBA public hearings Items 22 and 23) and voted unanimously to enter closed session.

votes.item_title: City Attorney Priority Item (Closed Session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3))
votes.notes: Voice vote carried unanimously; 6 votes were recorded on the day's Open Space & Trails Commission ballot (Howard Clement III was not recorded speaking in the digest).
votes.discussion_detail: City Attorney requested an additional closed session for attorney-client privileged consultation.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules for Triangle Transit Board of Trustees Reappointment (Item 3)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Suspended rules to vote immediately on Item 3 because the incumbent's term expired November 30 prior to the December 2 Council meeting.

votes.item_title: Triangle Transit Board of Trustees Reappointment (Item 3)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote (followed by another unanimous consent/item vote at 00:05:37).
votes.discussion_detail: Approved reappointment to the Triangle Transit Board of Trustees.

votes.item_title: Setting the Regular Council Meeting Agenda (Consent 1-2, 4-15, 17-19; GBA Public Hearings 22-23)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Set consent agenda for Items 1, 2, 4 through 15, and 17 through 19, and GBA public hearings for Items 22 and 23.

votes.item_title: Enter Closed Session
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Motion to convene in closed session as approved under the City Attorney's priority item.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting November 18, 2013
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Howard Clement III absent, the six-member Durham City Council moved efficiently through its November 18, 2013 agenda, approving all eight voting items unanimously (6-0). Council adopted the consent agenda, confirmed water and sewer assessment rolls on Ardmore Drive (granting a 20-year hardship payment plan) and Wedgewood Lane, and approved two major residential annexations and rezonings: Habitat for Humanity's Hope Crossing 2 development and the 33-lot Mineral Springs Road residential project. Council also approved a pulled appointment to the Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners after Mayor Bell explained Council's practice regarding appointment deferrals.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 5, 7-18, 32)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read the consent agenda, covering the 2014 council schedule, Rebound lease, mortgage loan servicing, employment and training grants, Church Street parking deck repairs, Human Services facility license, scrap tire recycling, vehicle-for-hire amendments, local transportation priority list, Mist Lake repairs, unauthorized water/sewer tampering ordinances, and police consulting services. Item 31 (Durham Housing Authority appointment) was pulled for separate consideration.

agenda_items.title: Mini Assessment Roll for Water Main on Ardmore Drive
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented a reconsideration of the water main assessment at 1012 Ardmore Drive following a timely financial hardship objection. In accordance with Council's financial hardship assessment policy, staff recommended confirming the original assessment amount with a 20-year payment period at 1% annual interest.

agenda_items.title: Confirmation of Assessment Rolls for Water Main and Sewer Main on Wedgewood Lane
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented water and sewer main assessment rolls for completed improvements benefiting properties along Wedgewood Lane. With no council questions or public speakers, Council closed the hearing and confirmed the rolls.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: Hope Crossing 2 (2800 Independence Avenue)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented Stewart Engineering's request on behalf of Habitat for Humanity to annex a 0.29-acre portion of 2800 Independence Avenue and apply initial RS-20 zoning so it could be incorporated into the 29-acre Hope Crossing 2 affordable housing development. Council Member Don Moffitt prompted staff to place the required legal notification certification on the record.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment: Hope Crossing 2 (A13-0004)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a Future Land Use Map amendment for the 29.9-acre Hope Crossing 2 site near Junction Road from Industrial and Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential, noting an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation. Council Member Steve Schewel asked about the location of planned city-owned additional athletic fields adjacent to the site.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change: Hope Crossing 2 (Z13-0011)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented the companion zoning map change for Hope Crossing 2, and council members discussed future street and pedestrian connectivity to the neighboring Midland Terrace development and city park property. Applicant representative George Stancil did not speak, and no opposition appeared.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: Mineral Springs Road Residential
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial PDR 4.14 zoning for up to 33 single-family homes on 9.09 acres of county enclave land on Mineral Springs Road. Council Member Diane Catotti inquired about Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission recommendations and pedestrian connections, while Council Member Steve Schewel requested offline clarification of the $165,000 net fiscal gain figure.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item: Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners Appointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After recognizing Boy Scouts in the audience, Council heard a public speaker praising the nominee's integrity and dedication to homeless, low-income, and disabled residents. Mayor Bell noted for the public record that Council customarily grants any council member's request to defer an appointment, before Council moved to approve the appointment.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Items 5, 7-18, 32; excluding pulled Item 31)
votes.notes: Howard Clement III absent. Item 31 was pulled for separate consideration (Mayor Bell initially misspoke 'Item 1' then clarified 'Item 31').
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell read the headings of the consent agenda items, which included the 2014 City Council meeting schedule, Rebound lease, mortgage loan servicing, employment and training grant ordinances, Church Street parking deck repairs, Human Services facility license, scrap tire recycling, vehicle-for-hire amendments, transportation priority list, Mist Lake repairs, water/sewer fee and tampering ordinances, and police consulting services. Item 31 regarding the Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners appointment was pulled from the consent agenda. Council approved the remaining consent items 6-0 with Howard Clement III absent.

votes.item_title: Item 23: Mini Assessment Roll for Water Main on Ardmore Drive (1012 Ardmore Drive)
votes.notes: Reconfirmed original assessment with 20-year payment period at 1% annual interest under financial hardship policy. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works Director Marvin Williams explained that after Council originally confirmed the Ardmore Drive water main assessment on September 3, 2013, the property owner at 1012 Ardmore Drive filed a timely hardship objection within the 15-day window. Under the City's Financial Hardship Assessment Policy, staff recommended confirming the original assessment amount while allowing repayment over 20 years at 1% annual interest. No council members raised questions and no members of the public spoke at the hearing. Council approved the mini assessment roll 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Confirmation of Assessment Rolls for Water Main and Sewer Main on Wedgewood Lane
votes.notes: Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented Item 24, requesting confirmation of water and sewer main assessment rolls for completed utility improvements along Wedgewood Lane. Staff confirmed that properties listed on the attached rolls had benefited from the new infrastructure. No council members asked questions and no members of the public spoke during the public hearing. Council adopted the resolution confirming the assessment rolls 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 25: Consolidated Annexation — Hope Crossing 2 (2800 Independence Avenue)
votes.notes: 0.29-acre voluntary annexation and initial RS-20 zoning for Habitat for Humanity Hope Crossing 2 development. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Pat Young presented the voluntary annexation and initial RS-20 zoning for a 0.29-acre portion of 2800 Independence Avenue east of Junction Road, submitted by Stewart Engineering on behalf of Habitat for Humanity to incorporate into its 29-acre Hope Crossing 2 project. Following a prompt from Council Member Don Moffitt, Young placed the required legal notice and affidavit certification on the record for all planning hearings. With no public speakers in opposition, Council closed the hearing and approved the annexation 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Comprehensive Plan Amendment — Hope Crossing 2 (A13-0004)
votes.notes: 29.9-acre FLUM amendment from Industrial and Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Future Land Use Map amendment A13-0004 for the 29.9-acre Hope Crossing 2 site near Junction Road in eastern Durham, changing the designation from Industrial and Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential. Staff and the Planning Commission (11-0) recommended approval. Council Member Steve Schewel asked staff to identify the location of city-owned land planned for additional athletic fields on Attachment 2, which staff confirmed lay immediately to the east. Applicant representative George Stancil offered no formal presentation, and Council approved the amendment 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Zoning Map Change — Hope Crossing 2 (Z13-0011)
votes.notes: Companion rezoning for Habitat for Humanity Hope Crossing 2. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff presented companion zoning case Z13-0011 for Habitat for Humanity's Hope Crossing 2 development. Discussion focused on street and site connectivity, with staff confirming that future connectivity would link to the adjacent Midland Terrace development once constructed as well as adjacent park property. Applicant representative George Stancil declined to speak further, and no public speakers opposed the rezoning. Council closed the public hearing and approved the zoning map change 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Consolidated Annexation — Mineral Springs Road Residential
votes.notes: 9.09-acre enclave annexation, utility extension, and PDR 4.14 zoning for up to 33 single-family homes. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented the utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial Planned Development Residential (PDR 4.14) zoning for up to 33 single-family homes on 9.09 acres surrounded by city limits on Mineral Springs Road, noting an 11-0 Planning Commission recommendation and positive fiscal impact analysis. Applicant Jarrod Edens stood by the staff report. Council Member Diane Catotti asked about Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission recommendations, and staff clarified that a pedestrian connection and right-of-way dedication were committed even though non-ordinance BPAC widening requests were not proffered. Council Member Steve Schewel asked staff to follow up offline on how Budget Management Services calculated the $165,000 cumulative net gain before Council approved the item 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 31 (Pulled): Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners Appointment
votes.notes: Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Council took up Item 31, the pulled consent item regarding an appointment to the Durham Housing Authority Board of Commissioners. A member of the public spoke in support of the nominee, praising her honesty and commitment to working with homeless, low-income, and disabled residents. Mayor Bell remarked for the public record that when any council member raises a question and requests a deferral on an appointment, it has been Council's longstanding practice to grant that deferral. Without further debate, Council approved the appointment 6-0.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Bill Bell, the Durham City Council approved priority items covering additional police headquarters consulting services (Item 32), referral of the Holloway Street Local Historic District expansion (Item 20), a closed-session legal consultation, and a supplemental Durham Housing Authority (DHA) Board appointment (Item 31). Council spent significant time debating potential revisions to the city's roadside solicitation ordinance based on Homeless Services Advisory Committee (HSAC) recommendations: Council Member Steve Schewel favored easing certain restrictions, whereas Diane Catotti, Don Moffitt, Eugene Brown, and Mayor Bill Bell raised traffic-safety, neighborhood-buffer, and legal drafting concerns—particularly opposing solicitation in active travel lanes or from the driver's side—and directed the City Attorney to refine draft language. On advisory board ballots, Jeffrey Scott Clark was recommended for the Human Relations Commission with 6 votes, while the DHA appointment produced a 5-1 split ballot with Larry Young receiving 5 votes and Lanier Foster receiving 1 vote (individual member ballot choices were not announced in the transcript). All procedural voice votes—priority items, setting the agenda, and entering closed session—passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items: Police HQ Consulting, Holloway Street Historic District, Closed Session & DHA Appointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items—supplemental Item 32 amending the consulting contract with Cardo Global Associates for police headquarters and referring Item 20 (Holloway Street local historic district expansion) back to administration—as well as the City Attorney's closed-session request and the City Clerk's supplemental Item 31 for the Durham Housing Authority Board.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Review & Citizens Comments on Development Review / Board of Adjustment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After reading through consent items (including Rebound Alternatives for Youth, WIA ordinances, Church Street parking deck repairs, Central Carolina Holding scrap tire contract, and water/sewer tampering ordinances) and public hearings (Hope Crossing and Mineral Springs Road annexations), Council heard citizens speak regarding limits on neighborhood testimony before the Development Review Board and Board of Adjustment as well as an applicant for board appointment.

agenda_items.title: Roadside Solicitation Ordinance & HSAC Recommendations Debate
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed Judge Marcia Morey's observations and Homeless Services Advisory Committee (HSAC) recommendations regarding the roadside solicitation ordinance. disagreements.issue: Roadside Solicitation Ordinance Revisions and Travel-Lane Safety
disagreements.summary: Council debated Homeless Services Advisory Committee (HSAC) proposals to relax portions of Durham's roadside solicitation ordinance, splitting between easing restrictions on solicitors and maintaining strict prohibitions against entering travel lanes or approaching driver-side windows.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support relaxing portions of the roadside solicitation ordinance in line with HSAC recommendations
side_a_arguments: Avoids overly punitive restrictions on panhandlers and addresses concerns raised in court proceedings
Incorporates months of collaborative work and recommendations from HSAC members directly engaged with homelessness issues
disagreements.side_b_position: Maintain strict street-safety rules barring solicitation in travel lanes and on driver-side vehicle approaches while tackling root causes
side_b_arguments: Placing panhandlers, student carwash bucket brigades, or any pedestrians in active travel lanes alongside 3,000-pound vehicles is unsafe
Approaching vehicles from the driver's side creates traffic hazards, and residential corridors like Club Boulevard and Duke Street need protection
HSAC's recommendations are not fully developed legally and require City Attorney drafting rather than weakening existing safety provisions
disagreements.resolution: No ordinance vote was taken; Council directed the City Attorney's office to work with staff and HSAC contributors to review legal options and draft specific language.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting November 4, 2013
meetings.executive_summary: In a brief 20-minute session on the eve of Durham's 2013 municipal election, the six-member Durham City Council (with Howard Clement III absent) issued a Pulmonary Hypertension Awareness Month proclamation and handled two voting items. During council announcements, Council Member Diane Catotti voiced personal objection to the bow-hunting deer ordinance on the consent agenda while voting yes solely because state law required unanimity, and Council Member Steve Schewel urged staff to explore adding Ninth Street bicycle racks under the CPGI Regency Erwin redevelopment amendment. Council approved the 16-item consent agenda 6-0 and granted water-main assessment relief until connection for three Valley Springs Road area properties 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Pulmonary Hypertension Awareness Month Proclamation and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell proclaimed November 2013 as Pulmonary Hypertension Awareness Month. Council Member Diane Catotti urged residents to vote in the November 5 municipal election and registered her personal opposition to the deer bow-hunting item (Item 9) despite voting yes due to state unanimity rules. Council Member Don Moffitt praised 300+ Oakwood playground volunteers, Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden announced the NCCU Prince Hall Shriners Diabetes Football Classic, and Mayor Bell welcomed visiting Kenyan filmmakers.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-16)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read the 16 consent agenda items, including board appointments, street acceptance, Wedgewood Lane assessment hearings, permit review audit, FY 2013-14 budget carryover, deer bow-hunting ordinance amendment (Item 9), CPGI Regency Erwin Development amendment (Item 10), SAMHSA grant, motor graders, water extension, stormwater repairs, and NCSU Triangle Regional Model support. Council Member Steve Schewel thanked staff for incorporating two of three BPAC recommendations in Item 10 and urged resolving NCDOT/ADA hurdles for Ninth Street bike racks.

agenda_items.title: Mini Assessment Rolls for Water Main in Valley Springs Road Area
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented continued assessment rolls for water mains on Valley Springs Road, Forestvale Drive, and Rose Road. Staff recommended finding that properties owned by John A.T. Foster, R&K Real Estate, and Bellis Browning had not benefited at this time and granting relief until they connect to city water at the prevailing frontage rate.

votes.item_title: Item 20: Mini Assessment Rolls for Water Main in Valley Springs Road Area
votes.notes: Granted relief until future connection for John A.T. Foster, R&K Real Estate, and Bellis Browning properties. Howard Clement III absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Public Works Director Marvin Williams presented Item 20, a continued public hearing on mini assessment rolls for water mains on Valley Springs Road, Forestvale Drive, and Rose Road. Staff recommended that Council find the properties of John A.T. Foster, R&K Real Estate, and Bellis Browning had not benefited from the water main improvements at this time and grant relief under the assessment relief policy, with prevailing water frontage charges due if the properties connect to city water in the future. meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Bill Bell, the Durham City Council unanimously approved Council Member Steve Schewel's motion to extend the timeline for the Durham Housing Authority (DHA) Board appointment by one week, heard a comprehensive DHA update detailing federal sequestration cuts (an 83% HUD operating subsidy equivalent to a $1 million loss and a 35% three-year drop in capital funds alongside a 9,200-9,600-person voucher waitlist), and held a lengthy policy debate on downtown and Ninth Street parking. On parking, Council members split on policy priorities: one member questioned maintaining a $2 million annual General Fund parking subsidy when competing against transit and affordable housing needs while urging a brief hold on a Ninth Street retail lease, whereas another member pushed back against 450-500 petitioners by arguing Ninth Street diners will pay for on-street parking and off-street lot capacity must stay protected for merchants, and another questioned charging full freight for covered residential spaces versus half-price surface spaces. Council referred Item 17 back to administration, approved the City Attorney's closed-session request, and set the consent and GBA public hearing agenda unanimously by voice vote.

agenda_items.title: City Attorney Closed Session Request & DHA Appointment Extension
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously approved the City Attorney's request for a closed session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3) for attorney-client consultation. Following the reading of the 23-item agenda—including the FY 2012-13 carryover amendment, a proposed deer bow-hunting ordinance amendment (Item 9), stormwater contract SD-2013-01 (Item 15), and Ninth Street/Downtown parking reports (Item 19)—Council unanimously approved Council Member Steve Schewel's motion to extend the DHA appointment window by one week.

agenda_items.title: Citizens Matters: Road Maintenance & John Tarantino
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident James Michael Lynch raised concerns regarding potholes, missing concrete and asphalt, and NCDOT maintenance restrictions on a local road, noting he had started a neighborhood petition. Resident John Tarantino also delivered musical public comment.

agenda_items.title: Durham Housing Authority (DHA) Annual Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: DHA leadership briefed Council on the impacts of the Budget Control Act and federal sequestration on its $39.2 million budget, including a 17% staffing reduction (23 positions), an 83% HUD operating subsidy pro-ration causing an estimated $1 million loss, and a 35% three-year decline in capital funding. DHA manages 15 sites and 1,867 units (135 managed by The Community Builders) plus 2,734 Housing Choice Vouchers with 9,200 to 9,600 households on the waiting list.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Downtown & Ninth Street Parking Study Reports
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council extensively debated parking fee structures, a 1992 parking resolution history, an unenforced $10 off-peak residential permit used 24/7 since 2004, Ninth Street paid on-street parking vs. retail lease obligations, a 'first hour free' option, and the city's $2 million annual General Fund parking subsidy. Members expressed differing views on the $2 million subsidy, Ninth Street merchant impacts, and covered-versus-surface residential parking discounts, while referring Item 17 back to administration.

agenda_items.title: Setting the Regular Council Meeting Agenda (Items 1-16 & 20)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After confirming Item 17 would be referred back to administration, Council voted to place Items 1 through 16 on consent and Item 20 (Valley Springs Road water main assessment) as a GBA public hearing item.

votes.item_title: City Attorney Priority Item (Closed Session under N.C.G.S. 143-318.11(a)(3))
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote among the five members answering initial roll call (Eugene Brown did not answer initial roll call, though he was referenced later at 03:12:45).
votes.discussion_detail: Approved City Attorney request for closed session consultation regarding legal actions.

votes.item_title: Extend Time for Durham Housing Authority Board Appointment by One Week
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Steve Schewel moved to extend the application/appointment period for the Durham Housing Authority Board for another week.

votes.item_title: Setting the Regular Council Meeting Agenda (Consent 1-16, GBA Public Hearing 20)
votes.notes: Passed by voice vote; automatic speech recognition rendered 'Seconded' and 'Aye' near the end as 'Senate'.
votes.discussion_detail: Set consent agenda for Items 1 through 16 and GBA public hearing for Item 20, while referring Item 17 back to administration.

disagreements.issue: Downtown Parking General Fund Subsidy, Residential Permits & Ninth Street Paid Parking
disagreements.summary: During review of the Downtown and Ninth Street parking studies, Council members expressed competing priorities over continuing the $2 million annual General Fund parking subsidy, how much to charge downtown residents for garage permits (including covered vs. surface spaces), and whether paid on-street parking on Ninth Street would harm local merchants.
disagreements.side_a_position: Question the $2 million parking subsidy relative to transit and affordable housing, and preserve Ninth Street lot access while holding the lease item briefly
side_a_arguments: Subsidizing $2 million a year for downtown parking represents an opportunity cost against competing priorities like transit fares and affordable housing
An off-street lot on Ninth Street is critical to East-side merchants, while on-street paid parking will not drive away customers despite 450-500 petition emails
Covered garage spaces warrant full-rate pricing compared to half-price surplus surface parking
disagreements.side_b_position: Support maintaining downtown parking affordability/incentives, examine 'first hour free' and employee permits, and investigate historical 1992 free-parking claims
side_b_arguments: Downtown residents raised concerns about $55-$65 monthly rates and 8 a.m.-6 p.m. off-peak restrictions
Clarifying whether any 1992 resolution promised free parking and evaluating a first-hour-free option or Ninth Street employee permits could soften merchant and resident impacts
disagreements.resolution: No final vote on parking rates was taken; Item 17 was referred back to administration and staff agreed to provide the 1992 resolution history and additional modeling.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting - Downtown Durham Vision Workshop
meetings.executive_summary: Chaired by Mayor Bill Bell ahead of the afternoon work session, this special City Council workshop reviewed the evolution of Downtown Durham planning and discussed policy priorities for managing rapid private development. Planning staff traced milestones from the 1989 revitalization plan and 2000 master plan through form-based zoning in the UDO, the 2007 Urban Design Center creation, the 2010 retail strategy, the 2012 Business Improvement District, and ongoing station-area infrastructure planning. In discussion, Council members expressed support for form-based zoning and denser skyline development while urging action on redeveloping surface parking lots, redesigning the Downtown Loop (including a tree-lined Morgan Street boulevard and pedestrian rail crossings), securing the Beltline Trail and intentional open space, and crafting targeted incentives for affordable housing and affordable retail without surrendering Council project-by-project review. Planning leadership cautioned that completing updated design guidelines depends on staff capacity and finalizing the Planning Department's annual work program through the Joint City-County Planning Committee; no formal votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: History of Downtown Durham Planning & Form-Based Zoning Overview
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff reviewed key milestones shaping downtown Durham—including the 1989 revitalization plan, 2000 master plan, 2001 downtown design overlay, 2005 comprehensive plan, 2006 UDO, 2007 streetscape projects and Urban Design Center, and 2012 BID and pedestrian workshops. Staff highlighted form-based regulations governing building height (300 feet by right in the core with unlimited height bonuses), active ground-floor facades, block sizes, and upcoming UDO and design manual updates.

agenda_items.title: Council Discussion: Urban Form, Loop Redesign, Open Space & Affordable Housing Incentives
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members endorsed form-based design standards while urging action on surface parking redevelopment, Downtown Loop boulevard redesign, pedestrian connectivity across rail lines, the Beltline Trail, and open space planning. Members also debated using targeted public incentives to achieve affordable housing (such as a 20% unit threshold) and affordable retail space ($12-$16/sq ft) while preserving Council and public-hearing review rather than creating an automatic blanket fund, as Planning staff noted staffing limits and a delayed annual work program.
